chapter_theme: Songs of Kundruthoradal (குன்றுதோறாடல், 'dancing on every hill'), Murugan of all the hills: a lovesick plea in the poet's own voice and one for a girl wasting with longing, a short prayer for refuge, a plea for the samadhi beyond yogis and sages, and a renunciation of praising miserly patrons for one word from Murugan's mouth; the praise names Murugan as the poet of Sambandar's victory over the Jains and as the one who settled the meaning of Pandya Tamil.
structure_note: 302 and 304 are love songs to Murugan (the first in the poet's own voice, the second for a girl); 303 is a short prayer; 305 sets women against yogic samadhi and is sung to the hill of Thirisiramalai; 306 renounces patron-praise. 302 names Thanigai and 305 Thirisiramalai, both gathered here under the heading of all hills.

302.reading: The poet asks that he not perish under the arrows of Kama's victorious cane bow, the moon spreading fiery light over the open street, the many parrot-tongued women skilled in slander, and the sounding wheel, but that Murugan, giving him devotion and granting release, come on the green peacock. The praise names the hero whose anklets are held in the heart of the dancer whose forehead eye burned, the chest that daily embraces the hunter girl, Murugan who always stands at Thiruthanigai, and the lord who freed the gods from the asuras' prison.
302.nuance: The poet borrows the lovesick girl's afflictions (Kama's arrows, the moon, the women's slander) for his own voice, and asks for பத்தி and முத்தி as the lover's cure. இசைபட்ட திகிரி is unclear; it may be the sounding conch or the moon's wheel. The shrine named is Thanigai, though the heading is Kundruthoradal.

303.reading: A short song: the poet asks when he will see the state in which he, bowing at Murugan's ringing anklets, takes refuge in him, and asks Murugan to dwell in his heart with compassion so that his troubles and doubts dissolve. The praise names him the son of Uma, who is part of the Lord who dances with none to rival him, and the one who plays in every town and dwells on many hills.
303.nuance: இடர் சங்கைகள் கலங்க: doubts as well as troubles are what grace should scatter. பலகுன்றிலும் அமர்ந்த: the song's close names the heading's sense, Murugan on every hill.

304.reading: Mostly praise: Murugan circled the seven worlds on his peacock in an instant, threw the vel for the gods, and spoke the one meaning of the Pandyas' Tamil so that it was honoured; within it the singer asks whether it is fitting that the girl who bows to his flower feet should droop with pallor and infatuation. The praise goes on to the old hill where the hunter girl pours out gems, pearls and coral from the stream, Murugan the guru who dwells in the hearts of those immersed in grace, and the lord of many hills.
304.nuance: வழுதியர் தமிழின் ஒருபொருள் அதனை வழிபட மொழியும்: Murugan declares the one meaning of the Pandyas' Tamil, perhaps the story of his judging the true commentary at the Madurai assembly, though the text names no more than this. The love plea is a single line set in the middle of the praise.

305.reading: The poet speaks of deceitful flirting women for whom men on earth write the madal, and asks whether he, a weak dog of a servant, should wilt and be deluded by their hair, breasts, waist, gait, speech and eyes; he asks Murugan to come and give him the samadhi and dissolution of mind, the secret bindu and nada reached by the swift filling of the breath, which true jnanis and silent sages cannot approach and which cannot be spoken, reached or thought. The praise names Murugan the hero on Thirisiramalai by the cool Kaveri from Kudagu, lord of the kurinji hunters, younger brother of the first Vinayaka, lord of the gods, guru of Gauri's lord, the master who dwells on all hills.
305.nuance: The plea is in the language of yoga: பவன பூரகம் (filling the breath), விந்து நாதம், சமாதி, மனோலயம். Yet the song says even jnanis and munis cannot reach it and asks it as a gift. மடல் எழுதும்: the women are those for whom men write the madal, the desperate lover's public plea. The praise is a litany of நாயக.

306.reading: The poet asks that he not perish in vain like the court bards who seek out the wealth and towns of deceitful, miserly fools, praising them in manjari, kovai, thoothu and many verse forms and arguing they are as generous as Pari and Kari, but that, chanting daily in Tamil Murugan's feet, anklets, kadamba garland, vel, peacock and six faces, he be given one word from the red mouth where wisdom springs. The praise names Murugan the learned one who gave the holy ash of wisdom that cured the Pandya's hunch and fever and sent the mute Jains to the stake with their peacock feathers, and the lord of Kundruthoradal whom the hill tribes worship with frenzied dance.
306.nuance: பாரி காரி என்று இசை வாது கூறி: the poet mocks the bard's stock claim that a miser is Pari or Kari, the legendary patrons. ஓர் சொல் அருள்வாயே: he asks for a single word, the guru's teaching. The praise identifies Murugan with Sambandar at Madurai: the Pandya's hunch (கூன்) and fever (தாபம்) cured by the ash, and the Jains (சமண்) impaled.

links.note: Both renounce the poet's trade of praising patrons; 292 quotes the comparisons he made, and 306 names the misers and the bards' claim that they are Pari and Kari, and asks instead for one word from Murugan.

The Kural begs those who beg not to beg of those who hide what they have; 306 confesses doing exactly that, praising misers as generous, and its answer is not to choose better patrons but to give patrons up for Murugan.
Both make Murugan the Tamil poet who sent the Jains to the stake, i.e. Sambandar; 299 adds the woman's husband brought back, 306 the Pandya's hunch and fever cured by the holy ash.

Tirumular teaches that bindu and nada, raised in the body, join in samadhi; 305 uses the same terms but says the state cannot be reached even by jnanis and silent sages, and asks Murugan to come and give it.

source_issues: Songs 302 and 305 name shrines (Thiruthanigai, Thirisiramalai) other than the heading குன்றுதோறாடல், which may be a collective heading for the hill shrines.
